---
title: "A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback"
---

Use the [tutorial](index.qmd) as a reference. These are paper-and-discussion
tasks, not specimen identifications or instructions for animal experiments.
Allow roughly 60–90 minutes including discussion. Leave with an annotated
comparison, a tissue-evidence table and a feedback diagram.

## 1. Put the boundaries back

Draw a nutrient's route from the mammalian gut lumen to the cytoplasm of a
skeletal-muscle cell. Include the absorptive epithelial cell, internal transport
fluid and muscle-cell membrane. Mark at least two places where selective
membrane transport matters. Explain why finding glucose in the gut lumen
does not establish that it has been absorbed.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

The gut lumen is continuous with the exterior. Name what lies on both sides
of each boundary; “goes into the body” is not a sufficiently precise arrow.
:::

## 2. Work the small geometry case

For hypothetical cubic bodies with side lengths 1, 2 and 4 mm, calculate
surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio. Give units for all
three. Then predict how characteristic diffusion time changes when a transport
distance rises from 0.1 to 1 mm, assuming the same medium and substance.

Explain why neither calculation proves that a large animal cannot exchange
enough oxygen. Name two structural/process changes that the simple cube lacks.
Show your arithmetic, not only the final ratio.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Numerical checkpoint

At 4 mm, area is 96 mm² and volume is 64 mm³. Check what happens when you
divide them. The tenfold distance change concerns a squared relationship.
:::

## 3. Recognise features before naming tissue

The following are invented descriptions, not observations from real slides.
For each, propose a primary tissue category, two supporting features and one
possible function. State what extra evidence would be needed to name an organ.

| Description | Features supplied |
| --- | --- |
| A | One thin layer of closely associated cells around a lumen; little intervening matrix |
| B | Widely spaced cells among abundant parallel extracellular fibres |
| C | Long, parallel, striated fibres containing multiple nuclei |
| D | Cell bodies with long processes among numerous smaller supporting cells |

Now explain why a circular empty-looking profile alone cannot identify a
blood vessel. Suggest how section angle could change a tubular structure's
appearance.

## 4. Repair a feedback explanation

A student writes: “When an animal gets hot, it sweats, so that is positive
feedback because sweating is helpful.” Rewrite this account using a regulated
variable, a disturbance, a sensor/control process, an effector and the effect
on the original deviation. Then identify two limits: not all animals sweat,
and evaporation depends on environmental conditions.

Draw the loop and label the arrow that opposes the initial disturbance.

## 5. Separate time scales and evidence

Classify each example as an acute response, an individual's acclimatory change,
or a proposed evolutionary adaptation. Explain the evidence needed for the
last classification.

1. Ventilation changes within minutes when an animal becomes active.
2. A fish's performance changes after several weeks at a new temperature.
3. A heritable gill feature is proposed to improve performance in a population's
   usual habitat over generations.

Would measuring a useful function in one individual be enough to establish
the feature's evolutionary origin? Explain.

## 6. Compare two solutions

Write 150–200 words comparing oxygen delivery in an insect and a mammal.
Include the environmental medium, exchange pathway, internal transport route,
two shared physical constraints and one trade-off. End with a measurement
that could test part of your explanation. Avoid ranking the animals as
“primitive” and “advanced”.

Finish with the [self-check quiz](quiz.qmd).
